title: Faire, prendre, mettre, dire
topic: present of faire, prendre, mettre, dire and their expressions
why: Faire, prendre, mettre and dire are four irregular verbs you'll use in almost every conversation. This lesson ties them to their everyday expressions, from household chores to the weather, and flags the forms English speakers get wrong, like vous faites and vous dites.

Faire: to do and to make

English needs two verbs, “to do” and “to make”. French has only one: faire. Je fais un gâteau (I'm making a cake), Je fais la vaisselle (I'm doing the dishes). It's irregular and extremely frequent, so learn it by heart.

faire
jefais
tufais
il, elle, onfait
nousfaisons
vousfaites
ils, ellesfont
  • Nous faisons is pronounced as if it were written “fe-zon”: the ai sounds like the e of le.
  • Vous faites and ils font are irregular: never “vous faisez” or “ils faisent”.

Household chores

FrenchEnglish
faire les coursesto do the grocery shopping
faire la cuisineto cook
faire la vaisselleto do the dishes
faire du sportto exercise, to play sports

In faire du sport, take du as part of the expression for now: you'll study it in unit 4.

The weather

The weather also uses faire, with an impersonal il that means “it”. Quel temps fait-il ? (What's the weather like? A fixed question with inversion.) Il fait beau (it's nice), il fait chaud (it's hot), il fait froid (it's cold), il fait gris (it's gray, overcast). Rain and snow have their own verbs: il pleut (it's raining), il neige (it's snowing).

Don't translate “it is cold” word for word: for the weather, always il fait froid, never “il est froid”. And when a person feels cold, French uses avoir: J'ai froid (I'm cold), like J'ai trente ans.

Prendre and its family

Prendre means “to take”, but it's also the verb for food, drinks and transport, where English says “have”, “get” or “catch”. Apprendre (to learn) and comprendre (to understand) are conjugated exactly the same way.

prendreapprendrecomprendre
je (j')prendsapprendscomprends
tuprendsapprendscomprends
il, elle, onprendapprendcomprend
nousprenonsapprenonscomprenons
vousprenezapprenezcomprenez
ils, ellesprennentapprennentcomprennent

The singular forms all sound the same, with a nasal vowel (the d of prend is silent). In the plural the nasal disappears: prenons, prenez, and prennent with a double n.

FrenchEnglish
prendre le train / le busto take (catch) the train / the bus
prendre un caféto have a coffee
prendre le petit-déjeunerto have breakfast
prendre une doucheto take a shower
apprendre le françaisto learn French
Le matin, je prends une douche, puis je prends le bus à huit heures.In the morning I take a shower, then I catch the bus at eight.

Probably the most useful sentence for a beginner: Je ne comprends pas. (I don't understand.) In speech you'll often hear Je comprends pas, without ne, but always write the full form.

", "

Mettre and dire

mettredire
jemetsdis
tumetsdis
il, elle, onmetdit
nousmettonsdisons
vousmettezdites
ils, ellesmettentdisent

Mettre keeps one t in the singular and two in the plural. Dire has the same trap as faire: vous dites, never “vous disez”.

  • Mettre = to put, to put on (clothes): mettre la table (to set the table), mettre un pull (to put on a sweater).
  • Dire = to say, to tell: dire bonjour (to say hello), dire que… (to say that…). English often drops “that”, French never drops que: Il dit qu'il pleut. (He says it's raining.)
Il fait froid : je mets un pull et je prends un parapluie.It's cold: I'm putting on a sweater and taking an umbrella.
Léa dit que vous faites la cuisine ce soir.Léa says you're cooking tonight.

To ask how to say something, use dire with on: Comment on dit « umbrella » en français ? — On dit « parapluie ». It's a sentence you'll use every day while learning.
